title: Why Your Class Must Be Hard
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening with the legend of Ernest Shackleton's ad for a hazardous expedition, Linsin argues that students are drawn to difficulty and challenge in the same way, and that making a classroom deliberately hard rather than easy is a powerful, underused way to build purpose and belonging. He connects this to SCM's existing principles around a compelling classroom students love, but singles out high standards specifically as the missing link tying classroom appeal to genuine specialness. The article warns that widespread post-pandemic efforts to lower standards in order to help students 'catch up' have the unintended effect of making school ordinary, which he argues students find unappealing and demotivating rather than relieving. He insists teachers should never lower standards, extend unlimited time, or pass students along unearned, arguing instead that raising the bar produces pride, confidence, discipline, and a sense of belonging to something remarkable. The piece closes with a rewritten version of Shackleton's ad recast for the classroom, framing challenge itself as the reward.
points: Opening with Ernest Shackleton's famously stark recruitment ad, the article argues students are drawn to challenge and difficulty in the same way explorers were drawn to hardship.
High standards are identified as the missing link connecting a classroom's appeal to genuine specialness and student motivation.
Widespread efforts to lower standards post-pandemic in order to help students 'catch up' inadvertently make school feel ordinary and demotivating.
Teachers should never lower standards, extend unlimited time on assignments, or pass students along unearned, regardless of pandemic-related setbacks.
Raising the bar produces pride, confidence, discipline, and a sense of belonging to something remarkable, which students find more appealing than ease.
quotes: Men wanted for hazardous journey. Low wages, bitter cold, long hours of complete darkness. Safe return doubtful. Honour and recognition in event of success.
We all want to be part of something bigger than ourselves. It’s a longing of human nature the best teachers, coaches, and business leaders use to motivate and inspire.
It makes school ordinary. And kids don’t like ordinary. None of us do. It inspires nothing. It makes even the idea of it exhausting. Unremarkable, mediocre, boring, easy, lazy, slow, soul crushing.
The truth is, you should never lower standards, for any reason. You should never give unlimited time for assignments, dumb down your curriculum, or pass along students unearned.

It provides meaning and self worth. It produces pride and confidence and discipline. It gives them something they’re unlikely getting anywhere else: The feeling of belonging to something remarkable and knowing that they have a higher purpose .
